slides.title: MATH 130
text: Properties, Measurements, and Formulas for Lines, Angles, and Surfaces

slides.title: Learning Goals
text: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
Identify acute, obtuse, right, and straight angles; find complements and supplements.
Use corresponding, alternate interior, and alternate exterior angle relationships to solve for unknowns.
Apply interior and exterior angle formulas for convex polygons with n sides.
Find areas of quadrilaterals and triangles using standard formulas including Heron’s Formula.
Use proportional reasoning to find unknown sides and angles in similar polygons; apply to real-world contexts.
Convert angles between decimal degrees and degrees-minutes-seconds (DMS) notation used in navigation.

slides.title: SECTION 1
text: Every geometric shape begins with points, lines, and angles — the atomic building blocks of all geometry.

slides.title: Undefined Terms in Geometry
text: Euclid attempted to define all geometric terms, but some definitions create challenges. We accept that point, line, and plane are undefined terms — we understand them intuitively.
A location in space with no dimension — no length, width, or height.
A straight path extending infinitely in both directions. Has length but no width.
A flat surface that extends infinitely in all directions. Has length and width but no depth.
Why “undefined”? Every definition requires prior terms. Point, line, and plane are the starting primitives — we build all of geometry on top of them.

slides.title: Geometric Notation Conventions
text: A straight path extending in both directions, no endpoints. Notation: AB with arrows above both ends (AB⇔) or line through AB.
Starts at endpoint A, passes through B, extends forever. Notation: AB with a right-pointing arrow above (AB→). Endpoint listed first.
A finite path connecting two endpoints A and B. Notation: AB with a bar above (AB̅). Has a definite, measurable length.
Two rays meeting at a vertex. Notation: ∠ABC where B is the vertex. Can abbreviate as ∠B if unambiguous. Measured in degrees.

slides.title: Congruence & Similarity
text: Use this notation consistently throughout the course.
Same shape and size. △ABC ≅ △DEF means identical in shape and size.
corresponding sides proportional. Order of letters in similarity statement matters!

slides.title: Rays & Angles
text: A half-line — starts at a point (endpoint) and extends infinitely in one direction.
Two rays sharing a common endpoint (vertex). The measure is the rotation from one ray to the other.
One complete rotation = 360° | Measured in degrees or radians | Protractor: tool for measuring angles
Initial Side (R₁): The starting ray of the angle
Terminal Side (R₂): The ending ray after rotation
Vertex: The common endpoint where both rays meet

slides.title: Measuring Angles
text: Angles can be measured in degrees or radians.
A protractor is an instrument used to measure angles (almost always in degree measure).

slides.title: Adjacent & Vertical Angles
text: Two angles that share a common vertex and a common side, but do not overlap.
Two angles formed by intersecting lines that are on opposite sides of the intersection.
∠AOB and ∠BOC are adjacent angles — they share vertex O and ray OB.
Vertical angles are always equal in measure (congruent).
Key Insight: When two lines intersect, they form two pairs of vertical angles. Each pair consists of congruent angles, and any two adjacent angles are supplementary (sum to 180°).

slides.title: Angle Relationship Map
text: Formed by intersecting lines; opposite each other; always congruent.
Share a vertex and a side; do not overlap; may or may not be supplementary.
Adjacent + supplementary; sum = 180°; on a straight line.
Any two angles whose measures sum to 90°.
Any two angles whose measures sum to 180°.
Key principle: Vertical angles are always congruent. All other relationships depend on position.

slides.title: Parallel Lines & Transversals
text: When a transversal crosses parallel lines, special angle relationships form:
Angles labeled 1–8 at two intersections: t is the transversal, l ∥ m are the parallel lines

slides.title: Corresponding Segments
text: When two transversals cross a pair of parallel lines, the segments between those parallel lines are called corresponding segments.
If l₁ ∥ l₂ ∥ l₃ , then segments a, b are corresponding and c, d are corresponding.
a / b = c / d and equivalently a / c = b / d

Assuming the vertical lines are parallel, use proportions to find unknown distances. Worked Example: if a = 6, b = 9, c = 8, find d. Step 1 — Set up: a/b = c/d → 6/9 = 8/d. Step 2 — Cross-multiply: 6d = 9 × 8 = 72. Step 3 — Solve: d = 12.

slides.title: Solving Angle Equations: Method
text: Are the angles equal, supplementary (180°), or related by position?
Corr./alt.int./alt.ext. → set equal. Co-interior → sum to 180°.
Step 3 — Solve for x, then find the angle
Isolate the variable, then substitute back to get the degree measure.
Step 4 — Check with supplementary if needed
Adjacent angles on a straight line sum to 180°. Use this to find the supplementary angle if asked.
Works for any angle pair from parallel lines:
Corresponding, alt. int., alt. ext. → equal

text: Given: l ∥ m, cut by transversal t.

slides.title: Example: Parallel Lines & Angles
text: Lines l and m are parallel, and t is a transversal.
Given ∠2 = 2x + 19° and ∠7 = 3x + 2°, find the measure of ∠1.
Step 1: Identify the relationship — ∠2 and ∠7 are alternate exterior angles (equal).

slides.title: SECTION 2
text: Polygons & quadrilaterals build on angle relationships from Section 1 — now we measure enclosed area and classify shapes.

slides.title: Polygons
text: A polygon is a closed region of a plane bounded by three or more straight line segments. Sides must be non-collinear and non-self-intersecting (no crossings). Formulas below apply to convex polygons.
speaker_notes: Diagram: Right Triangle — the two shorter sides are legs a and b; the side opposite the right angle (longest side) is hypotenuse c. Mark the right angle with a small square at the corner.

slides.title: Polygon Angle Formulas
text: These formulas apply to convex polygons with n sides.
Sum of Exterior Angles = 360° (always, for any convex polygon)
Each Interior Angle of a Regular Polygon = (n − 2) × 180° / n

slides.title: Interior Angle Sum Formula
text: Any polygon can be divided into triangles by drawing diagonals from one vertex.
A polygon with n sides produces (n − 2) triangles.
Each triangle has an angle sum of 180°.
Formula: (n − 2) × 180° where n = number of sides

slides.title: Exterior Angle Sum
text: Key Fact: Sum of Exterior Angles = 360° (always, for any convex polygon)
One exterior angle at each vertex. The sum is always 360°, regardless of the number of sides.
Each interior angle of a regular n-gon = (n − 2) × 180° / n
Each exterior angle of a regular n-gon = 360° / n
Interior + exterior angle at any vertex = 180° (linear pair)
Pentagon (5): interior = 108°, exterior = 72° | Hexagon (6): interior = 120°, exterior = 60°
Octagon (8): interior = 135°, exterior = 45° | Decagon (10): interior = 144°, exterior = 36°
Note: interior + exterior = 180° (always, at every vertex — linear pair)

slides.title: Types of Quadrilaterals
text: Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel
A diagonal of a polygon is a line segment joining any two nonadjacent vertices.

slides.title: Area of Quadrilaterals
text: Area is given in square units (ft², m², mi², cm², in²) | Rhombus: A = d₁ × d₂ / 2 (d₁, d₂ = diagonals)

slides.title: Examples: Area of Quadrilaterals
text: b₁ = 3.6 ft, b₂ = 5.5 ft, h = 2.9 ft
Always label units: area is always in square units (cm², ft², m²). Forgetting units costs points on the quiz.

slides.title: Worked Example: Multi-Step Trapezoid
text: Key strategy: when the height is not given, look for a right triangle hidden in the trapezoid. Use the Pythagorean theorem to find h first, then apply A = ½(b₁ + b₂)h.

slides.title: Compound Shapes Strategy
text: Identify simple shapes within the compound figure (rectangles, triangles, trapezoids).
Ensure all necessary measurements are identified for each part.
Apply the correct formula to each piece separately.
Add areas of parts (or subtract holes/cutouts).
Always express area in square units (cm², ft², m², etc.).

slides.title: Application: Area of Compound Shapes
text: The wall of a living room with a vaulted ceiling has 3 windows as shown.
If a quart of paint covers 80 ft², how much paint is required to paint these walls?
Step 1: Wall = rectangle + triangle on top
Step 2: Find each area, then subtract 4 windows
Step 3: Net wall area ÷ 80 ft² per quart = quarts needed
See diagram for exact dimensions → answer varies by wall size.

slides.title: SECTION 3
text: The most important polygon — every other polygon can be divided into triangles.

slides.title: Types of Triangles
text:
No two sides are equal in length.
No tick marks on sides.

Two sides are equal in length.
Shown with single tick marks on equal sides.

All three sides are equal.
Shown with double tick marks. All angles = 60°.
Has one right angle (90°). The side opposite the right angle is the hypotenuse; the other sides are legs.

slides.title: Triangle Properties
text: The three interior angles of any triangle always sum to exactly 180 degrees.
The total distance around the triangle — sum of all three side lengths.
A triangle is exactly half of a parallelogram with the same base and height. The height (h) is the perpendicular distance from the base to the opposite vertex.

slides.title: Triangle Area: Decision Guide
text: A = ½bh — Use when base and height are known
Height must be perpendicular to the base. Works for all triangle types.
All three sides equal (s). Derived from the 30-60-90 split.
Heron's Formula — Use when only all three sides are known
No height needed — powerful when height is unknown.
Decision rule: Know height? → ½bh. All equal? → equilateral. Only sides? → Heron's.
Know height? → Use ½bh | All sides equal? → Use equilateral formula | Only sides? → Use Heron's
Heron's is the most versatile — it works for any triangle when all three side lengths are known.

slides.title: Heron's Formula
text: Use this when the height isn’t known — it only requires the three side lengths. When you know all three side lengths but not the height, use Heron’s Formula to find the area.
Triangle with sides a = 4.5 mi, b = 5.6 mi, c = 8.2 mi

slides.title: Equilateral Triangle Formula
text: For an equilateral triangle with side s:
2. Base of each = s/2, hypotenuse = s

slides.title: Application: The Bermuda Triangle
text: The Bermuda Triangle is sometimes defined as an equilateral triangle 1600 km on a side, with vertices in Bermuda, Puerto Rico, and the Florida coast.
Assuming it is flat, what is its approximate area?

slides.title: The Pythagorean Theorem
text: For a right triangle: the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the two legs.
a, b = legs (the two shorter sides)
If a² + b² = c² → right angle (opposite c)
If a² + b² > c² → angle opposite c is acute (triangle is acute)
If a² + b² < c² → angle opposite c is obtuse (triangle is obtuse)
Example: Box is 13 × 10 in with diagonal 16.75 in. Is it square? 13² + 10² = 269, but 16.75² = 280.5625. Since 269 < 280.56, the angles are obtuse — not right angles.

slides.title: The Scarecrow’s “Theorem”
text: The correct theorem (a² + b² = c²) is NOT the Scarecrow’s “theorem” from The Wizard of Oz — he said:
“The sum of the square roots of any two sides of an Isosceles triangle is equal to the square root of the remaining side.”
He got his diploma anyway — but his geometry was wrong.
The Pythagorean Theorem states a² + b² = c² for ANY right triangle — not just isosceles.
On the quiz: identify the hypotenuse first (opposite the right angle), then apply a² + b² = c² correctly.

slides.title: Error Analysis: Triangle Area
text: Mistake 1 — Using the slanted side as height
The height must be perpendicular to the base. A slanted leg is NOT the height unless the triangle is right-angled.
Mistake 2 — Forgetting to square the units
Area is always in square units. 12 cm × 8 cm = 96 cm², not 96 cm.
The hypotenuse is always opposite the right angle — the longest side.
Mistake 4 — Applying Heron's with the wrong s
s is the semi-perimeter: s = (a+b+c)/2, not a+b+c.

slides.title: SECTION 4
text: Similarity extends triangle properties to proportional reasoning — two shapes with equal angles have predictable side length ratios.

slides.title: Similar Triangles
text: Two polygons are similar if they have the same shape (but not necessarily the same size).
Corresponding angles are equal in measure.
We write △ABC ~ △DEF to denote similarity. Only 2 pairs of equal angles are needed to prove similarity.
Given △MNP ~ △QRS, use corresponding angles to find missing angles (they sum to 180°), and set up proportions like MN/QR = NP/RS = MP/QS to find missing sides.

slides.title: Similarity: Strategy
text: Confirm AA (Angle-Angle) similarity. Order of vertices in the statement matters.
Scale factor = (side of one figure) / (corresponding side of other figure).
a/b = c/d — corresponding sides in the same ratio.
Step 5 — Interpret: label with units, verify the ratio holds.
Common shortcut: If two angles are known equal, the third must be equal too (angle sum = 180°).
Scale factor > 1: figure is enlarging. Scale factor < 1: figure is shrinking. Always state which direction.

slides.title: Applications: Similar Triangles
text: A 6 ft man stands 10 ft from a flagpole. His 8 ft shadow ends at the same point as the flagpole's shadow.
BC ∥ DE. AB = 50 ft, AD = 180 ft, BC = 60 ft. Find DE (river width).
Strategy: Identify the two similar triangles → match corresponding sides → set up the proportion → cross-multiply and solve.

slides.title: Application: Parallel Segments
text: Two parallel lines are cut by two transversals. Segments AB = 9, BC = 6, and DE = 12. Find EF.
Strategy: Parallel lines always divide transversals in the same ratio. Identify corresponding segments before setting up the proportion.

slides.title: Error Analysis: Similarity
text: Mistake 1 — Wrong order in similarity statement
△ABC ~ △DEF means A↔D, B↔E, C↔F. Swapping letters changes which sides correspond.
If AB/DE = BC/EF, do NOT flip one side: AB/DE ≠ EF/BC.
Mistake 3 — Mixing sides from different triangles
Always keep numerators from one figure and denominators from the other.
Mistake 4 — Confusing the scale factor direction
Larger → smaller: scale factor < 1. Smaller → larger: scale factor > 1.
Quick check: Write out the similarity statement first, then list corresponding pairs before setting up any ratio.
If your answer gives a scale factor < 0 or makes sides negative, you have a ratio error — flip and retry.

slides.title: SECTION 5
text: Navigation, surveying, and GPS express angles in degrees-minutes-seconds — here we connect that real-world notation to our angle work.

slides.title: Degrees, Minutes & Seconds
text: Conversions are on the next two slides.
Angles in navigation, surveying, and GPS use degrees-minutes-seconds (DMS) — here’s how to convert. Used in navigation, latitude/longitude, and aviation approach plates.

slides.title: Decimal Degrees → DMS
text: Step 1 — The whole number part is the degrees
Step 2 — Multiply the decimal remainder by 60 → minutes
Step 3 — Multiply that decimal remainder by 60 → seconds

slides.title: DMS → Decimal Degrees
text: Step 3 — Add all three parts together
Common mistake: forgetting to add all three parts. The answer is 120 + 0.8 + 0.01389, not just 120.01389 or 0.81389.

slides.title: Angles in Navigation: The Nautical Mile
text: Historically, one nautical mile was defined as the distance of one minute of latitude (at sea level).
A ship traveling 10 nautical miles covers 10 × 1852 = 18,520 m ≈ 18.5 km

slides.title: Core Geometric Competencies
text: By the end of this unit, you should be able to do all of the following:
Classify angles (acute, right, obtuse, straight). Apply vertical, supplementary, and parallel line relationships. Write and solve angle equations.
Derive and apply (n−2)×180° for interior sums. Use 360° for exterior sums. Find individual angles in regular polygons.
Apply formulas for squares, rectangles, parallelograms, trapezoids, and rhombuses. Partition compound shapes. Choose the correct triangle formula (½bh, equilateral, Heron’s).
Identify similar polygons using AA. Write correct similarity statements. Determine scale factors and set up proportions to find missing sides.
Convert decimal degrees to DMS (multiply remainders by 60 twice). Convert DMS to decimal (divide by 60 and 3600, then add). Understand the nautical mile connection.

slides.title: Quiz Preparation: Key Skills
text: Find missing angles and sides using proportions (△MNP ~ △QRS)
Identify corresponding, alternate interior, and alternate exterior angles
Use A = ½bh, equilateral formula, and Heron's formula
Break complex shapes into parallelograms and rectangles, sum the areas
A = ½(b₁ + b₂)h — identify bases, height, and any diagonal measurements
Remember: Show all work for full credit! Label your units.

slides.title: Practice Checklist
text: Before the assessment, make sure you can:
Identify all parallel line angle pairs by name and state their relationship (equal or supplementary).
Find interior and exterior angle sums for any polygon, and solve for missing angles.
Partition compound shapes, apply correct formulas, give answers in square units.
Write correct similarity statements, calculate scale factors, set up and solve proportions.
Convert decimal degrees ↔ DMS accurately. Understand the nautical mile connection.
